sections.html: Xenomystus nigri is the smallest Old World knifefish. It usually grows to 12-15 cm, exceptionally to 20 cm. It lacks a dorsal fin, which distinguishes it from all other Old World knifefish.
The species is widely distributed in western Africa. The photographs show a juvenile specimen from the Congo and two adults from the Niger River in Nigeria, from where they are usually obtained.
In nature it feeds mainly on insects and worms. In the aquarium, it readily accepts all common frozen foods, but will also accept dry foods.

Very small fish are eaten by African knifefish; they are peaceful to all larger fish. They are crepuscular animals, as can be seen from their large eyes. In the aquarium Xenomystus do not necessarily want caves, but dim shelters.
The sexes are hardly distinguishable; males are a bit more high-backed.
Xenomystus nigri are crevice spawners, "shooting" their eggs individually into depressions or small holes. The species does not seem to take broodcare.

Knifefishes inspire above all by their elegant swimming. The special fin structure allows them to maneuver both forward and backward, and they are lightning fast. They are intelligent, get to know the keeper and come to receive tidbits on whistle. Among themselves they communicate with sounds and "electric speech", using weak electrical impulses. Although the fish is not colorful, it is a wonderful contrast fish to other aquarium inhabitants.
